title: Points & Vectors
description: Represent points and vectors, and use the dot and cross products that power geometry

blocks.text: Computational geometry starts with two objects: points and vectors. Almost every geometry algorithm, from checking intersections to building a convex hull, is built on a small set of operations on them.
The two operations that matter most are the dot product and the cross product. Master these and the rest of geometry becomes far more approachable.
A point is a location, written as a pair of coordinates like (x, y). A vector has the same form but represents a direction and length, an arrow, rather than a fixed spot.

The vector from point A to point B is simply B minus A, subtracting coordinate by coordinate. This tiny operation, turning two points into the arrow between them, is the start of nearly every geometry routine.

items: A point is a position given by coordinates
A vector is an arrow with direction and length
The vector from A to B is B minus A
Prefer integer coordinates to keep computations exact

blocks.text: Vectors add and subtract component by component. Geometrically, adding places them tip to tail, and the sum is the arrow from the very start to the very end.

blocks.caption: Vectors add tip to tail; subtraction gives the arrow between two tips

blocks.text: Subtraction gives the arrow pointing from one tip to another, which is how we turn points into direction vectors in the first place.
The dot product of two vectors multiplies matching components and adds them: a.x times b.x plus a.y times b.y. The result is a single number that measures how much the two vectors point the same way.

blocks.caption: The dot product measures alignment; the cross product measures turn and area

items: Positive means the vectors point in broadly the same direction
Negative means they point in broadly opposite directions
It also gives projections and the angle between vectors

blocks.text: The cross product in 2D is a.x times b.y minus a.y times b.x. It gives a signed number equal to the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors.
Its sign is the real prize: it tells you whether b lies to the left or the right of a. That single fact drives orientation tests, polygon area, and convex hulls.

The most useful primitive:

The sign of the 2D cross product answers "which way do we turn?" It is the backbone of almost every geometry algorithm you will write.
A compact point type with a few helpers covers most needs. Keep coordinates as integers when you can, so the dot and cross products stay exact.

codes.python:
# a point or vector is just a tuple (x, y)
def sub(a, b):   return (a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1])
def dot(a, b):   return a[0] * b[0] + a[1] * b[1]
def cross(a, b): return a[0] * b[1] - a[1] * b[0]

blocks.text: These primitives are the foundation of the geometry topics that follow.

items: Orientation tests, using the sign of the cross product
Polygon area, using a sum of cross products
Angle and projection questions, using the dot product
Convex hull and segment intersection, using both

blocks.text: Everything else in geometry is these few operations, combined in clever ways.
